name: I LIKE WALNUTS AND I CANNOT LIE BURGER (comes with walnut pesto)

recipe.history:
The walnut — Juglans regia, the English or Persian walnut — is one of the oldest tree nuts in human consumption, with fossilized evidence of walnut eating in the Périgord region of France dating back sixty thousand years to Neanderthal occupation. The walnut tree is native to a broad swath stretching from the Balkans through Central Asia to China, and its cultivation is documented in records from ancient Persia and the Fertile Crescent going back at least four thousand years. The Romans called it Juglans regia — the royal nut of Jupiter — and spread its cultivation across their empire, bringing walnut trees to Britain, France, Germany, and the Iberian Peninsula. In medieval Europe, the walnut was prized for its oil (used in cooking, lamps, and paint — Rembrandt is thought to have used walnut oil in many of his paintings), its timber, its dyeing properties, and of course its flavor. Walnuts appear in the oldest written recipe for pesto-like sauces: the ancient Roman moretum described by Virgil was a paste of herbs, cheese, garlic, and nuts, and the medieval agliata was a walnut-garlic sauce used throughout Italy and France. In Liguria, where basil pesto famously originated, there exists a parallel tradition of salsa di noci — walnut sauce — made with blanched walnuts, garlic, olive oil, bread, and sometimes Parmigiano Reggiano, used to dress pasta, particularly the pasta pockets called pansoti. Salsa di noci predates basil pesto in the written record and represents one of the oldest continuously made nut-based sauces in European cooking.

Walnuts arrived in North America through multiple routes. Native black walnuts (Juglans nigra) were already present in abundance and had been eaten by Indigenous peoples for thousands of years; their flavor is more intense and slightly more bitter than the Persian walnut, and they remain a beloved ingredient in Midwestern and Appalachian cooking. European settlers brought Persian walnut trees with them, and by the 19th century California had established itself as a major walnut-producing region — today, California produces over 99% of commercially grown walnuts in the United States. Walnut pesto — a variation on the Ligurian salsa di noci — entered American restaurant culture through the Italian-American culinary tradition and the farm-to-table movement's embrace of nut-based sauces as an alternative to dairy-heavy preparations. Walnut pesto is richer, more robust, and slightly more bitter than basil-pine nut pesto, with a complexity that comes from the walnut's natural tannins and the depth of their toasted flavor. On a burger, walnut pesto functions as both sauce and garnish: its richness complements the beef, its herbal freshness cuts through the fat, and its textured, chunky consistency provides something to bite through.

Walnuts have been a constant in my cooking for as long as I can remember cooking at all, partly because my grandmother kept a bowl of them in the shell on her kitchen table year-round, a nutcracker always nearby. The ritual of cracking walnuts — the satisfying snap, the slightly bitter smell, the particular challenge of extracting the meat in large pieces — was a meditative activity of winter afternoons. I learned early that toasting walnuts — a dry pan over medium heat, stirring constantly until the nuts deepened in color and their oils became fragrant — transformed them from merely good into something remarkable: nuttier, more complex, with a faint roasted quality that made them taste more intensely of themselves. When I first made walnut pesto, I was struck by how the toasting and the blending worked together to produce a sauce with a depth of flavor that basil pesto, for all its brightness, didn't quite reach. Walnut pesto has a gravity to it, a richness, a slight bitterness at the edges that I find more interesting than the cleaner, brighter flavors of a summer herb pesto. It belongs on a burger the way it belongs on pasta: emphatically and without apology.

Walnut pesto is a rich, fat-forward sauce — olive oil, walnut oil, ground nuts — and it requires a medium rare patty at 130–135°F to be properly appreciated. The fat in the pesto wants the fat in the beef to be equally present and expressive, and a medium rare patty delivers exactly that. The juice that runs from a medium rare patty as you bite through it mixes with the oil of the walnut pesto to create a combined richness that is deeply satisfying; a dry, well-done patty has no juice to contribute, and the pesto sits on top of it rather than intermingling. Beyond the practical, there is a philosophical point here that I feel strongly: cooking a burger to medium rare is an act of respect for the animal whose life produced that beef. It is a commitment to doing justice to the ingredient, to cooking it at the temperature where all of its qualities are most fully expressed. Every cook who has tasted a medium rare burger next to a well-done one and been honest about the difference knows this. The walnut pesto simply makes the case more eloquently.
ingredients: 1 tbsp olive oil (for hands and pan)
1½ cups walnut halves and pieces, toasted
2 cups fresh basil leaves, loosely packed
½ cup fresh flat-leaf parsley leaves
½ cup good-quality extra-virgin olive oil, plus more as needed
2 tbsp walnut oil (or substitute more olive oil)
½ cup freshly grated Parmigiano Reggiano
3 tbsp walnuts, toasted and finely chopped
Salt and white pepper to taste
¼ cup toasted walnut halves (for garnish)
instructions: 1. Roast the garlic for aioli: Preheat oven to 400°F. Slice the top ¼ inch off a head of garlic to expose the clove tips. Drizzle with 1 tsp olive oil, wrap in foil, and roast 40–45 minutes until the cloves are completely soft and golden. Cool, then squeeze the roasted garlic out of the skins into a bowl and mash to a smooth paste.

2. Make the ciabatta-style buns: Dissolve yeast in warm water with sugar. Let stand 5–10 minutes until foamy. In a stand mixer with dough hook, combine bread flour and salt. Add yeast mixture and olive oil. Knead on medium 10 minutes — the dough will be quite wet and shaggy; this is correct. Increase to medium-high and knead 5 more minutes until smoother and beginning to pull from the bowl. Do not add more flour. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and let rise at room temperature 2 hours until more than doubled and full of bubbles.

3. Generously oil a rimmed baking sheet. Pour the wet dough onto the oiled sheet and, using oiled hands, gently stretch it into a rough rectangle about 10x12 inches. Dimple the surface thoroughly with your fingertips. Drizzle lightly with olive oil and sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Cover loosely and proof 45 minutes. Preheat oven to 450°F. Bake 20–25 minutes until deep golden and crisp on the bottom. Cool on a rack, then cut into 6 portions. Slice each horizontally.

4. Toast the walnuts: Spread walnut halves in a dry skillet over medium heat. Toast, stirring frequently, 4–5 minutes until fragrant, slightly darkened, and beginning to smell nutty. Watch carefully — they can burn quickly. Transfer to a plate to cool.

5. Make the walnut pesto: Place toasted walnuts, basil, parsley, and garlic in a food processor. Pulse 8–10 times until roughly chopped. With the machine running, slowly stream in olive oil and walnut oil until the pesto reaches a textured, slightly chunky consistency — do not process to a smooth paste; some texture is essential. Transfer to a bowl and stir in Parmigiano Reggiano, Pecorino, lemon juice, salt, pepper, and red pepper flakes. Taste and adjust — the pesto should be bold, slightly bitter, herbaceous, and rich. Add a splash more olive oil if too thick. Press plastic wrap directly onto the surface to prevent oxidation.

6. Make the walnut-herb compound butter: Beat softened butter until fluffy. Fold in finely chopped toasted walnuts, thyme, rosemary, lemon zest, salt, and pepper. Mix until thoroughly combined. Roll in plastic wrap into a log shape and refrigerate until firm, at least 30 minutes. Slice as needed for basting.
7. Make the roasted garlic aioli: Whisk together mayonnaise, roasted garlic paste, and lemon juice until smooth. Season with salt and white pepper. Refrigerate until needed.
8. Form patties: Gently mix ground beef with salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Divide into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Shape into ¾-inch-thick patties with a center dimple.

9. Cook patties: Heat a cast iron skillet or flat-top over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3–4 minutes on the first side without pressing. Flip. Add a slice of walnut-herb compound butter to the pan and baste patties continuously with the foaming herbed butter for 1–2 minutes. Add Provolone or Fontina to each patty and cover briefly to melt. Remove when internal temperature reads 130–135°F for medium rare. Rest 3 minutes.
10. Toast buns: Melt butter in a skillet over medium heat and toast buns cut-side down 2–3 minutes until golden and crisp.

11. Assemble: Spread roasted garlic aioli on both cut sides of each bun. Spoon a generous tablespoon of walnut pesto directly onto the bottom bun. Place the medium rare patty with melted cheese on the pesto. Add a slice of ripe tomato. Add a small handful of baby arugula. Spoon another tablespoon of walnut pesto over the arugula. Scatter 4–5 toasted walnut halves on top. Add a few fresh basil leaves. Finish with flaky sea salt and a small pinch of lemon zest. Cap with the top bun (spread with a thin layer of walnut pesto on the inside) and serve immediately.
